parole.significato: flaó (a kind of pie or tart in Catalan cuisine, usually filled with cheese and sweetened with honey)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin fladō, from Frankish *flaþō. Doublet of flam.

parole.significato: to bloom, to blossom, to flower
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre.
Inherited from Old Catalan fogaça, from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”).
Inherited from Late Latin follicāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin fōmentāre.
Inherited from Old Catalan fenoll~fenoyll, from Late Latin fēnuculum, alteration of Latin fēniculum, diminutive of fēnum (“herb”). Compare Occitan fenolh, French fenouil, Spanish hinojo.
From forn (“oven”) + -er (“occupational suffix”), or Late Latin furnārius, from Latin furnus.
Borrowed from Late Latin fortificātiōnem, from fortifico, from Latin fortis.
Borrowed from Late Latin fortificāre, from Latin fortis.
Inherited from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”). Compare Occitan fòrça and archaic French force (adjective).
From Late Latin Francus, perhaps via Old French franc.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

parole.significato: lights (lungs of an animal eaten as food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin frixūra, from frīgō (“to fry”).
Inherited from Late Latin fructa, from Latin fructus.
Borrowed from Late Latin francicus.

Inherited from Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium, probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”). Compare Occitan fuèlha (Old Occitan folha), French feuille, Spanish hoja.
Borrowed from Late Latin fumigātiōnem, from Latin fumigō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin funda (“bag”). Doublet of fona.
Borrowed from Late Latin fūnerārius (“pertaining to a funeral”), from Latin funus.
Inherited from Late Latin furōne, fūrō (“thief”). Compare Spanish hurón.
Inherited from Late Latin fusta (“beam”), from Latin fustis, with a change in gender. See also the dialectal or archaic fust.

parole.significato: to flog, whip, lash, beat with force
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin fustigāre, from Latin fustis.
Inherited from Late Latin gaius. Cognate with French geai.
Borrowed from Late Latin galilaea, from Latin Galilaea.
From Late Latin gambărus, from cammărus, from Ancient Greek κάμμαρος (kámmaros, “lobster”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ganglion, from Ancient Greek γᾰγγλῐ́ον (gănglĭ́on).
Inherited from Late Latin garrulāre, denominal from Latin garrulus (“overly talkative”).
Presumably a derivation from Late Latin gaza (“treasury, wealth, riches”), from Ancient Greek γάζα (gáza, “treasury, treasure”), from Old Median *ganǰam (“treasure”).
Inherited from Old Catalan gat, from Late Latin cattus (“cat”). Compare Occitan gat~cat, French chat, Spanish gato.
From Late Latin zēlōsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Inherited from Old Catalan genoyll (and numerous other variants), from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.
Inherited from Old Catalan gingebre, from Late Latin gingiber, from Latin zingiberī.
From Late Latin iectāre, from Latin iactāre. Cognate with French jeter.

parole.significato: to dare (to have enough courage to do something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan osar, from Late Latin ausāre, frequentative based on Latin audeō. The initial /ɡ-/ may have been appended to resolve hiatus in phrases such as no (g)osar. Compare Aragonese gosar, Occitan ausar.
Inherited from Late Latin grassus.

parole.significato: a caparison which covers the croup and flanks of a horse, mule, etc.
parole.testo: From Late Latin vastrapes, from a language of Southwestern Asia.
From Late Latin gubia, from Gaulish *gulbiā. Cognate with English gouge.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin habitāculum. Doublet of bitàcola.
Inherited from Late Latin haereticus. Doublet of herètic, which was borrowed.
From Late Latin histriōnicus (“pertaining to acting”), from Latin histriō (“actor”).
From Old Catalan ivern, from Late Latin hībernum.

parole.significato: to horrify, horripilate, give the creeps
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin horripilāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin hospitālis, hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), noun use of Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of the inherited hostal.
Borrowed from Late Latin hospitālārius. Equivalent to hospital + -ari.

From Old Catalan hostal, from Late Latin hospitāle (“shelter, hospice, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“of a host or guest; hospitable”), from hospes (“host, guest”). First attested in the 13th century.
From Late Latin humiliātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin Hunni.
Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Borrowed from Late Latin idoneitāte, idōneitās (“usefulness”).
Borrowed from Late Latin illuminātiōnem, from Latin illuminō.
Borrowed from Late Latin imbricāre.
From Late Latin immediātus (“immediate”).
Borrowed from Late Latin impartīre (as a variant of impertiō), from Latin partiō.
From Late Latin impeccābilis.
From Late Latin imperturbābilis.
From Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”). First attested in 1490.

parole.significato: impostor (someone who uses a false identity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin impostōrem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin impostūra, possibly via French imposture.
From impuls, or borrowed from Late Latin impulsāre, from Latin impulsus.
From Late Latin inaccessibilis.

parole.significato: to set on fire; (figurative) to inflame
parole.testo: From Late Latin incendiare.
Borrowed from Late Latin incestuōsus.
Borrowed from Late Latin incomplētus, from Latin complētus.
Borrowed from Late Latin inculpāre.
From Late Latin incurābilis. First attested in 1460.
Borrowed from Late Latin indēfīnītus.
From Late Latin indīcibilis.
From Late Latin indiscrētiōnem.
From Late Latin īnfectiō.
Borrowed from Late Latin iniūriāre, from Latin iniūriārī.
Borrowed from Late Latin innovātiōnem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin inquilīnātus.
Borrowed from Late Latin īnspirātiōnem, from Latin īnspirō.
Borrowed from Late Latin interruptōrem, from Latin interrumpō.

parole.significato: to title (give a title to a work)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin intitulāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin inventārium.
From Late Latin invīsibilis.
From Late Latin irascibilitātem.
Borrowed from Late Latin irrēgulāris.
Borrowed from Late Latin itinerantem.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin itinerārium.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin itinerārius.
Borrowed from Late Latin hierarchia.
Inherited from Late Latin diurnum. Doublet of diürn, a borrowing.
Borrowed from Late Latin Ioviālis.
From Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós).

parole.significato: to Judaize (convert to the Jewish religion or conform to Jewish culture)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaīzāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūrāmentum, from Latin iūrō (“swear”). By surface analysis, jurar + -ment.
Borrowed from Late Latin justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from Latin iustus.
Borrowed from Late Latin iūstificāre, from Latin iūstus.
Borrowed from Late Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβῠ́ρῐνθος (lăbŭ́rĭnthos, “maze”).
Borrowed from Late Latin labyrinthĭcus. By surface analysis, laberint + -ic.
Borrowed from Late Latin lēctūra, from Latin lēctūrus.
Borrowed from Late Latin Levīta.
From Late Latin limitrophus.
Borrowed from Late Latin litterālis.
Inherited from Late Latin lamprēda, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: to throw (to cause an object to move rapidly through the air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan lançar, from Late Latin lanceāre 'hurl (a spear)', from Latin lancea (“spear”) (whence Catalan llança), of Celtiberian origin. First attested in the 14th century. Compare French lancer, Italian lanciare, Occitan and Portuguese lançar, Spanish lanzar.
Inherited from Late Latin lotō, from Latin lotus, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós, “lotus”).

parole.significato: legua, Spanish league, a traditional unit of distance equivalent to about 4.2 km
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin leuga (“Gaulish mile”). Cognate with Spanish and Galician legua and Portuguese légua.
Borrowed from Late Latin legūminōsus.
Inherited from Old Catalan let, leyt f, from Late Latin lactem, from Latin lac n. First attested in the 14th century. Compare Occitan lach, lèit, lait and Aragonese leit, let, llet.

parole.significato: to liberate, to emancipate, to free
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lībertō (“I liberate”).
Inherited from Old Catalan litera, from Late Latin lectuāria, derived from Latin lectus (“bed”). By surface analysis, llit + -era.

llogar (obsolete form of lloc (“place”)) + -et (diminutive suffix). From Late Latin locālem, from Latin locus. Doublet of local. Compare with Aragonese lugar, with the same meaning. Also compare Galician lugar, Portuguese lugar, Asturian llugar, and Spanish lugar, with a different meaning.
From Late Latin lurdus, from Latin lūridus. Compare Italian lordo (“dirty”).
Inherited from Late Latin lūmināria, neuter plural of lūmināre, from Latin lūmen. Doublet of lluminària, a learned borrowing.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin lūmināria, nominative/accusative plural of lūmināre (“luminary; lamp”). Doublet of llumenera.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin laudemium influenced by the suffix -isme.

Most likely simply from Late Latin lendina, variant of lendinem, from Classical Latin lendem. The unexpected /m/ (instead of */n/, the usual outcome of Latin /-nd-/) may be due to analogy with another word- or simply dissimilation from the following /n/.
Borrowed from Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. First attested in 1803.
Borrowed from Late Latin lumbāgō.
Inherited from Late Latin mātrastra (“stepmother”), from Latin māter (“mother”).
Inherited from Late Latin malitātem.

Inherited from Old Catalan melancolia, from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”). The metathesis of the vowels may be due to influence from mal (“bad”).
From Late Latin maniaticus, derivative of maniacus.
First attested in 1803. Uncertain origin, perhaps from Late Latin maniacus (“maniac”), in this sense first applied to spoilt children. Later it came to denote docility.
From Late Latin maniacus, from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós).
Inherited from Late Latin marcīre, from Latin marcēre.

parole.significato: tenant farmer and steward of a mas
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin mānsuārius (“steward”, later with insertion of -v- to break hiatus), from Latin mānsus.
Probably an extension of Late Latin matta (“mat”), i.e. "mat-like growth of plants".

parole.significato: enrollment, registration (in a course, a team, a club)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin mātrīcula, from Latin mātrīx.

Inherited from Old Catalan maça, from Late Latin mattia or Vulgar Latin *mattea, probably from Latin mateola, from Proto-Indo-European *mat (“hoe, plow”). Compare Occitan massa, Spanish maza, Portuguese maça, French masse, Italian mazza.
Borrowed from Late Latin mediālis.
Inherited from Old Catalan meitad, from Late Latin medietātem, a noun based on Latin medius (“middle, half”). Compare Occitan meitat~mitat.
Inherited from Late Latin mēlum, variant of mālum (“apple”).
Inherited from Old Catalan melon, from Late Latin mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepōnem, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”).
Borrowed from Late Latin mentālis, from Latin mēns; equivalent to ment + -al.
Shortening of Old Catalan dementre, from Late Latin dum interim.

parole.significato: mistral (cold northwest wind from the Atlantic)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan maestral, from Late Latin magistrālis. Doublet of magistral, a learned borrowing.
Inherited from Old Catalan mesurar, from Late Latin mēnsūrāre, derived from Latin mēnsūra (“measurement”).
From Late Latin metallizō, from metallum (“metal”).
Inherited from Old Catalan mellorar, from Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin meliārī (“better”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ministeriālis. By surface analysis, ministeri + -al.
Inherited from Late Latin minuāre, from Classical Latin minuere.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin myops, from Ancient Greek μύωψ (múōps).
From Late Latin myriadem, from Ancient Greek μυριάδος (muriádos), genitive of μυριάς (muriás, “number of 10,000”), from μύριος (múrios, “numberless, countless, infinite”).

parole.significato: to mediate, to broker, to act as a middleman
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin *mediantāre, from Latin mediāre (“to be in the middle”).
Inherited from Old Catalan molí, from Late Latin molīnum (“mill”), a noun derived from Latin molere (“grind”). Compare Occitan molin, French moulin, Spanish molino.
Borrowed from Late Latin monachālis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin monachismus.
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).
From Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχίᾱ (monarkhíā).
Inherited from Old Catalan monjo~monje, from Late Latin monicus, alteration of monachus.
From Late Latin monogamia. By surface analysis, mono- + -gàmia.
Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis, from Latin monumentum; equivalent to monument + -al.
From Late Latin monasticus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin Mosaicus.
Inherited from Late Latin muscātus, from mūscus.
From Late Latin muttum (“sound”), from muttire (“mutter, make a mu-noise”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare French mot.

parole.significato: A unit of land area defined as the amount that a team of oxen could plow in a day, roughly equivalent to an acre.
parole.testo: From Late Latin modiāta, from modius (“measure”). Equivalent to muig + -ada.
Borrowed from Late Latin mundiālis.
Inherited from Late Latin montāniōsus, an adjective based on montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”). By surface analysis, muntanya + -ós.
Inherited from Late Latin muralia, from Latin muralis.
From Late Latin mūsellum.
Borrowed from Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
Inherited from Late Latin nārīcem, ultimately derived from Latin nāris.
From Late Latin natica, an adjectival term based on Latin natis (“rump, buttock”). Cognate to Italian natica.
From Late Latin nātūrālitātem. First attested in 1492.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin necrōsis, from Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis).
Derived in masculine from the feminine neta, from Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis (“granddaughter”). Compare Portuguese neto and Spanish nieto.
Inherited from Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis. Compare Spanish nieta.
Inherited from Late Latin nigella, substantivization of the feminine of Latin nigellus (“blackish”), so-named on account of its tiny black seeds.
Inherited from Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”).
Inherited from Late Latin nūtrīcia.
From Late Latin (arbor) nucāria, from Latin nux.
Inherited from Old Catalan oca, from Late Latin auca, syncopated from *avica, from classical Latin avis (“bird”). Compare Occitan auca, French oie, Spanish oca.

Inherited from Old Catalan aucell, oceyl, from Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis. Cognate with Occitan aucèl, French oiseau.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ochra, from Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “yellow”). The spelling with -e is due to influence from French ocre.
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía). By surface analysis, oligarca + -ia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarca (“oligarch”) + -ic (adjective-forming suffix).
Borrowed from Late Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía).
Borrowed from Late Latin operāre. Doublet of obrar, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Late Latin operātōrius, from operātus. Equivalent to operar + -tori.
From Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós).
Borrowed from Late Latin orīginārius. Cognate with Occitan originari, French originaire, Spanish originario.
Inherited from Late Latin ossuōsus, an adjective based on Latin os (“bone”). By surface analysis, os + -ós (for /-s-/, cf. the plural ossos 'bones').
From oir + -ible, or from Late Latin audibilis.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin ōidium.
Borrowed from Late Latin palpābilis.
Borrowed from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
Borrowed from Late Latin partiālis.

parole.significato: matching; a group of two with the same characteristics
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan parell~pareyll, from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Occitan parelh, French pareil, Spanish parejo.

parole.significato: pair (set of two people or animals intended to do something together)
parole.testo: Substantivization of the feminine of Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Spanish pareja.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin parentēla.
Inherited from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m.
From Late Latin parochialis.
From Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía).
From Late Latin particularitātem.
Borrowed from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of paraula, which was inherited. The mathematical sense is taken from New Latin or directly from Greek.

parole.significato: parenthesis (clause or word inserted into a passage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
Inherited from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin paternitās.

Borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Byzantine Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).
From Late Latin patrōnātus.
From Late Latin peculiaritātem.
Borrowed from Late Latin peciolus, variant of petiolus (“little foot; fruit stalk, stem, petiole”). Doublet of peçol.
Inherited from Late Latin (sē) paenitīre, from Latin paenitēre.
From Late Latin pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ, “fiftieth”).
Borrowed from Late Latin perceptibilis (from Latin percipiō), equivalent to percebre + -ible.
Inherited from Old Catalan perdonar, from Late Latin perdōnāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin perinaeum.
Borrowed from Late Latin perpendiculāris, from perpendiculum.
Borrowed from Late Latin persōnālis.
Inherited from Late Latin per hoc (“for this reason”, literally “through this”). Compare Spanish pero, Italian però.
From Late Latin pettia, from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis. Compare French pièce, Italian pezza, Spanish pieza.
Inherited from Late Latin pedōnem (literally “pedestrian”), derived from ped- (“foot”). Compare Spanish peón, French pion.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pyrōpus, from Ancient Greek πυρωπός (purōpós, “fire-colored”)
Borrowed from Late Latin planetārius.
Inherited from Old Catalan plantar, from Late Latin plantāre.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin plasmātiō. By surface analysis, plasmar + -ció.
Inherited from Late Latin plagia. Cognate with Galician praia, French plage, Italian spiaggia, Occitan plaja, Portuguese praia, and Spanish playa.
From poblar + -ció or a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin populātiōnem from Latin populus (“people”).
Inherited from Old Catalan pooll~peoll, from Late Latin pēduculus.
From Late Latin porcārius. By surface analysis, porc + -er.
From Late Latin portātōrem.

Inherited from Old Catalan posar, from Late Latin pausāre (“halt, rest”), likely influenced in meaning by Latin pōnere ("put"; cf. inflections such as posui). Doublet of pausar, a borrowing from Latin.
From Late Latin pragmaticus, from Ancient Greek πραγματικός (pragmatikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin prandiālis or Latin prandium.
Borrowed from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus.
Borrowed from Late Latin praefīxum, from Latin praefīxus.
Borrowed from Late Latin praescientia.
Borrowed from Late Latin praesentiālis.
From Late Latin praesidentiālis, from praesidēns.
Inherited from Late Latin praestus, from the Latin adverb praestō. Compare French prêt, Italian and Spanish presto.
Borrowed from Late Latin praevisiōnem.
Inherited from Late Latin prīma vēra, derived from Latin prīmus (“first”) + vēr (“spring”).
Borrowed from Late Latin proclāmātiōnem, from Latin proclāmō.
Borrowed from Late Latin productivus.

parole.significato: program, plan, schedule (a set of structured activities)
parole.testo: From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).
Borrowed from Late Latin prōiectāre (compare Italian proiettare, Spanish proyectar), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō.
From Late Latin prōlongātiōnem.
Borrowed from Late Latin prōnōminālis.
Borrowed from Late Latin propīna.
Borrowed from Late Latin prōstibulum (“brothel”).
from Late Latin proselytus (“proselyte, alien resident”), from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos, “newcomer, convert”)
From Late Latin prōtectiōnem.
Inherited from Old Catalan prou, from Late Latin prōde (“profitable”), rebracketed from Latin prōdest (“is useful”). Compare French prou.
Deverbal from provar, possibly corresponding to Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin psōriasis.
Inherited from Late Latin puncta, from the feminine of Latin punctus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin pūrgātīvus, from pūrgāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin purgātōrium (“cleansing”).
Borrowed from Late Latin putatīvus.
Inherited from Old Catalan polvora, polvera, from Late Latin pulvera, neuter plural based on Latin pulvis m. Doublet of pols < *pulvus.

Inherited from Old Catalan quaranta, from Late Latin quarranta, from Latin quadrāgintā (“forty”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥(d)ḱomt (“four-ten”). Compare Occitan quaranta, French quarante, and Spanish cuarenta.

parole.significato: Lent (period of penitence for Christians before Easter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin quadragēsima. Doublet of quadragèsima, a learned borrowing.
From Late Latin cherūbīm, plural of cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), from Hebrew כְּרוּב (kerúv).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin chymus, from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).
Borrowed from Late Latin quaestionārius, from quaestiono, from Latin quaestiō.
From Late Latin rabbī.
From Late Latin ratiōnālitātem.
Borrowed from Late Latin raphē, from Ancient Greek ῥαφή (rhaphḗ, “seam”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ratiōnābilis and adapted to raó, from Latin ratiōnem. Equivalent to raó + -able.
From earlier rasor, from Late Latin rāsōrium.

parole.significato: rashness; sudden action taken without forethought
parole.testo: Along with Occitan rauja (“rage”) from Late Latin rabia from Classical Latin rabiēs (“rage”). The appearance of x in place of j likely due to raixa (“a violent emotion”). Doublet of ràbia.

parole.significato: a bunch or cluster of fruit of a common infructescence, especially of grapes
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan raïm~razim, from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus (“bunch, especially of grapes”).
Borrowed from Late Latin reālis, from Latin rēs.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin recollēctāre, frequentative of recolligō.
Inherited from Late Latin retorta.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin refectōrium.
Inherited from Late Latin liquiritia (via metathesis), from glycyrrhiza, a borrowing of Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza).
Borrowed from Late Latin regimentum.
Borrowed from Late Latin rēgulāris.
From regular + -itat, or borrowed from Late Latin rēgulāritātem.
Borrowed from Late Latin reiterāre.

Probably from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin regia, from Latin porta regia ("royal gate"), with later influence from Arabic رِيشَة (rīša, “batten”). Alternative etymologies suggest Vulgar Latin *regla, from regula, although Catalan rella is the proper descendant of this word.
From Late Latin reliquia.
Borrowed from Late Latin reminīscentia (“remembrance”), from Latin reminīscēns, present active participle of reminīscor (“to remember”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin renalis, from Latin rēnēs (“kidneys”).
Inherited from Old Catalan reentar, from Late Latin recentāre, from Latin recentem (“new”).

parole.significato: to replace (to restore to a former place)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin repausāre, from Latin pausāre.
Borrowed from Late Latin reprehēnsibilis.
Inherited from Old Catalan respondre, from Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre. The modern Catalan conjugations reflect contamination from the unrelated pondre (“lay, set”).
Borrowed from Late Latin restrictiōnem, from Latin restringō.
From Late Latin retrogradare.
